title: Predict-then-optimise interchange control for rail logistics with combined passenger-freight chains
abstract: Interchange decisions at rail transfer stations directly affect end-to-end service reliability and cost-to-serve; yet, existing delay-management approaches either forecast delays without prescribing actions or optimise dispatch with coarse delay representations. We propose a predict-then-optimise framework that integrates multi-task LSTM-based delay prediction with a feasibility-constrained Markov Decision Process (MDP) to determine whether to proceed, hold, reschedule, or reroute services at transfer stations. The LSTM models short-horizon delay propagation using only information available at the prediction epoch, while the MDP converts the predicted delay class, capacity regime, infrastructure condition, and bounded dwell feasibility into auditable dispatch recommendations. We evaluate the framework on a three-leg regional rail case study in central Germany comprising lines RB5 (Fulda–Bebra), RB87 (Bebra–Eichenberg), and RB83 (Eichenberg–Kassel), with two physical interchange stations (Bebra and Eichenberg). The results show that the sequence models provide sub-minute ETA accuracy across all three legs and that the Bebra interchange policy reduces the cost-to-serve index by 7.0% relative to the earliest-feasible heuristic while maintaining the same structural miss rate under a 60-minute admissible dwell window. At Eichenberg, the MDP and earliest-feasible policies perform almost identically among evaluable journeys, while the low matched-departure coverage highlights a data and timetable-coordination limitation for full multi-leg evaluation. The framework contributes a deployment-oriented closed-loop architecture in which policy-induced connection gaps are propagated into downstream ETA estimation, supported by per-timestep station embeddings, two-stage cross-leg fine-tuning, and replay-buffer stabilisation. The paper demonstrates how established prediction and control components can be operationally coupled to provide interpretable, manager-facing rail logistics decision support with journey-level KPIs and cost-to-serve reporting.

title: Behavioral influences in hedging decisions for commodity purchasing
abstract: Hedging in commodity purchasing involves securing commodity prices or quantities in advance to protect against price fluctuations and reduce financial risk. This paper examines the impact of risk-taking attitude, confidence level, and numeracy skills on a supply manager’s hedging decisions in commodity purchasing. We employ a discrete choice experiment to test four hypotheses grounded in existing literature. The experiment was designed through extensive consultations with industry practitioners and refined through a pilot study. Using data collected from 136 sourcing managers in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) industry, we find that the hedging decisions are significantly influenced by a combination of risk-taking attitude, confidence, and numeracy skills. Risk-taking and confidence are positively associated with riskier hedging choices, while numeracy shows a weaker, negative direct effect, primarily moderated by risk-taking and confidence. These findings deepen our understanding of how specific behavioral traits impact hedging decisions in commodity purchasing, offering practical insights for firms to better align managerial risk preferences with organizational risk management strategies, particularly in volatile market environments.

title: Integrating prompt-based zero-shot learning into Bayesian network for maritime cybersecurity risk analysis
abstract: The increasing digitalisation of maritime ecosystems, including vessels, ports, offshore facilities, and shore-based organisations, has expanded the attack surface of maritime operations and increased exposure to cyber threats. Cyber incidents affecting these interconnected systems may propagate across global logistics networks, highlighting the need for systematic cybersecurity risk analysis in maritime transport. However, existing studies often rely on expert judgement or limited datasets, which restrict scalability and hinder comprehensive identification of Risk Influential Factors (RIFs). This study develops a data-driven framework that integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted text classification with Bayesian Network (BN) modelling to analyse maritime cybersecurity risks. A structured taxonomy of RIFs is defined to capture temporal, regional, operational, and technical attributes of cyber incidents. LLM-based prompt engineering is then employed to automatically extract these factors from unstructured incident reports. The reliability of the automated classification process is evaluated through manual annotation on a sampled subset of incident reports and comparative experiments across multiple LLMs. The BN model is further assessed using repeated cross-validation to evaluate predictive performance and robustness. The results reveal key dependencies among cyber incident characteristics and consequence types, providing probabilistic insights into maritime cyber risk patterns. The proposed framework offers a scalable approach for analysing cyber risks in maritime transport systems and supports risk-informed cybersecurity management.

title: Pricing and frequency decisions in RoRo-road freight competition: A multi-leader game-theoretic model
abstract: This paper proposes a game-theoretic framework to study competitive interactions between road transport and Short Sea Shipping in Roll-on/Roll-off (RoRo) cargo services. We model the interaction as a multi-leader-common-follower game, where sea and road operators set prices, and the sea operator also adjusts service frequency. Shippers respond using a logit-based choice model where utility depends on price and transit time. We compute the solution through an iterative best-response procedure that converges to a Nash equilibrium among leaders within a Stackelberg hierarchy between leaders and followers. Computational experiments on three European corridors (Gothenburg-Ghent, Cuxhaven-Immingham, and Rosslare-Dunkirk) explore scenarios with varying cost structures and customer sensitivities. Results show that sea transport generally gains market share, but profitability is notably stronger when price sensitivity is low. When price sensitivity is high, operators face challenges unless frequency increases are applied strategically, particularly in settings with high time sensitivity, since higher frequency reduces waiting times and attracts sufficient additional demand to maintain competitiveness. We introduce a frequency-viability index, which signals when an additional weekly sailing is economically justified. These findings highlight the strategic role of pricing and frequency in promoting modal shift and suggest that policy support may be necessary for long-term competitiveness.

title: Generative AI and Machine learning collaboration for container dwell time prediction via data standardization
abstract: Import container dwell time (ICDT) prediction is a key task for improving productivity in container terminals, as accurate predictions enable a reduction in container rehandling operations by yard cranes. Achieving this objective requires accurately predicting the dwell time of individual containers. However, the primary determinants of container dwell time are recorded as unstructured text, limiting their effective use in machine learning models. To address this limitation, this study proposes a collaborative framework that integrates generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) with machine learning. The proposed framework employs Gen AI to standardize unstructured information into standard international codes, with dynamic re-prediction triggered by electronic data interchange state updates, thereby enabling the machine learning model to predict ICDT accurately. Extensive experiments conducted on real container terminal data demonstrate that the proposed methodology achieves a 13.88 % improvement in mean absolute error over conventional models that do not utilize standardized information. Furthermore, applying the improved predictions to container stacking strategies achieves up to a 13.07 % reduction in the number of relocations, thereby empirically demonstrating the potential of Gen AI to enhance productivity in container terminal operations. Overall, this study provides technical and methodological insights into the adoption and effectiveness of Gen AI in port logistics.

title: Experience-driven value creation in digital airline self-service systems: evidence from a low-cost carrier context
abstract: This study examines an experience-driven value creation mechanism in digital airline self-service systems in the low-cost carrier (LCC) context. It focuses on a setting less frequently studied in customer experience research: digitally mediated, low-contact airline services in which booking, check-in, and boarding interfaces function as customer touchpoints embedded in standardized passenger-service processes. From a passenger logistics perspective, these interfaces are part of standardized passenger-service systems through which customers complete sequenced service tasks with limited employee contact. Drawing on means-end theory and service-dominant logic, the study models customer experience (CX) as an antecedent of customer-perceived value (CPV) and behavioral intentions (BIs). Survey data were collected from 330 passengers of a European LCC operating in France and were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The analysis reports positive and statistically significant CX → CPV and CPV → BIs effects. The main empirical evidence concerns the indirect CX → CPV → BIs path, whereas the direct CX → BIs path is small in magnitude. In the final model, the CPV composite comprises utilitarian value/control and emotional value. No statistically significant generational cohort moderation is detected in this sample, and robustness checks indicate that the mediated CX → CPV → BIs path remains positive and statistically significant when value-for-money perceptions and travel frequency are considered. The study applies CX theory to low-contact airline environments and examines digital self-service interfaces as passenger touchpoints within standardized LCC service processes. For managers, the results underscore the importance of CX in digitally mediated LCC journeys and direct attention to interface clarity and low-friction task completion.

title: How construal level can shape buyer responses to supplier labor violations
abstract: Despite widespread organizational commitments to eliminate labor exploitation in supply chains, a substantial gap persists between stated policies and suppliers’ actual practices. Major companies pledge zero tolerance for labor violations at suppliers, yet evidence that buyers follow through with meaningful corrective action when suppliers commit labor violations has been limited. This gap between commitment and enforcement of labor policies by buyers reduces supplier compliance and undermines efforts to improve working conditions in global supply chains. We address the problem of buyer follow-through by exploring whether construal can influence buyers’ responses to supplier labor violations. Construal level is an established driver of managerial behavior in many domains, yet exploration of its role in supply chain decision-making is limited. Using three experiments we show that reducing construal can improve the relationship between buyer responsibility for its suppliers’ workers and buyer willingness to suspend the supplier for a major labor violation. Our findings contribute novel insights for more effective governance of working conditions in supply chains, by: i. identifying that construal can influence buyer willingness to respond to supplier labor violations; and ii. identifying interventions that influence construal and elicit more effective buyer action, including faster reporting, clear labor policies, concrete thinking, and increased expertise. Our research emphasizes the important role of construal in supply chain decision making and its links to managerial understanding of working conditions in supply chains. Our findings advance efforts to encourage more effective action from buyers when labor violations are reported in their supply chain.

title: Deep reinforcement learning for optimizing mobile depots allocation and hybrid order dispatch in last-mile delivery under multi-participants behavioral uncertainty
abstract: As last-mile delivery demand continues to grow and customer preferences become increasingly diverse, traditional single-mode logistics systems are inadequate in addressing the complexity and variability of modern urban delivery environments. In this paper, we propose an innovative hybrid last-mile delivery system that leverages mobile depots as intermediate hubs, integrating crowd-shipping, and customer self-pickup, to enhance cost-effectiveness. However multiple stakeholders in the system have conflicting interests, ignoring their behavioral uncertainties can impair operational efficiency and increase delivery costs. For example, customers and crowd-shippers may compete for the limited storage capacity of mobile depots, and crowd-shippers may be unwilling to deliver orders that customers decline to pick up. Specifically, the study captures crowd-shippers’ order-acceptance behavior and customers’ self-pickup choice through two binomial logit models, and embeds these behavioral components into a stochastic mixed-integer programming model. This model jointly optimizes mobile depots allocation and order dispatch decisions, aiming to minimize the expected total operational cost. Considering computational complexity of this model, we propose PRiME-DQN, a reinforcement learning framework that incorporates behavior-prioritized resource filtering, action biasing, and model-efficient temperature tuning to accelerate convergence and improve solution quality. A case study on Amazon’s last-mile delivery in Seattle shows that the proposed hybrid model achieves up to 49.5% cost reduction in low-shipper settings and 11.3% in higher-shipper settings compared to a crowd-shipping system, while also consistently surpassing the self-pickup baseline by 3–6%. Extensive scaling experiments show that PRiME-DQN produces high-quality feasible solutions efficiently. For the largest instances, it achieves delivery costs 1.97% lower than Gurobi’s best incumbent solution obtained within the 3,600-second time limit, while reducing the solution time to approximately 1400 seconds.

title: Integrating minimum cost flow and capacitated location in global supply chains under uncertainty
abstract: Modern supply chain networks face significant challenges in balancing operational efficiency and resilience under diverse real-world uncertainties such as demand fluctuations and disruptions. To address these complexities, this study proposes an Integrated Capacitated Facility Location and Minimum Cost Flow Problem under Multi-Uncertainty (ICLMF-MU). The integrated multi-objective optimization model simultaneously optimizes total cost, service utility, and total risk while accounting for unmet demands and disruptions in supply chain network design. To deal with the NP-hardness of the problem, we propose an enhanced hybrid non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II). A novel bi-level evaluation strategy couples an exact linear programming (LP) solver to maintain flow balance with a greedy heuristic as a fallback mechanism. Through a three-stage benchmarking process, the algorithm demonstrates strong convergence and consistent performance. A large-scale numerical study (100 nodes) evaluates performance under diverse global trade environments, contrasting cost-sensitive goods against strategic resources prone to export controls. Pareto frontier trade-off analysis identifies a distinct Criticality Premium, confirming that strategic sectors require a substantially greater investment to withstand sanctions compared to commercial scenarios. Furthermore, regret analysis exposes a Robustness Paradox: the min-risk strategy exhibits the highest operational regret and lowest real-world resilience by limiting network scope. In contrast, the max-utility and balanced strategies demonstrate superior robustness. Sensitivity analysis confirms this implicit redundancy provides the structural capacity needed to absorb large demand surges, with the medical strategy demonstrating superior overall resilience under extreme demand. These findings imply that for critical supplies, true robustness is an emergent property of sufficient capacity investment rather than the optimization of theoretical risk indicators alone, offering guidance for designing resilient networks in an unstable global trade landscape.

title: Route-aware detection of ship collision avoidance manoeuvres via change point analysis with intention inference
abstract: Reliable and human-consistent collision avoidance is essential for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) operating in mixed traffic environments. A key challenge is the extraction of representative critical encounter scenarios from real-world data without relying on predefined risk thresholds or expert-driven rules. This study proposes a data-driven, route-aware framework for detecting ship collision avoidance behaviours and extracting the critical encounter scenarios in which such behaviours occur. The framework comprises three components. First, ship motion patterns are analysed to characterise normal route-following behaviour, enabling collision avoidance behaviour to be distinguished from routine navigation. Second, a unified cost function is formulated to jointly evaluate multiple kinematic features while explicitly incorporating planned route information, enabling separation of route-following course changes from potential avoidance actions. Change Point Detection (CPD) method is then applied to identify behavioural transitions and segment ship trajectories into candidate collision avoidance manoeuvres. Third, an intention-informed encounter identification approach is introduced, where avoidance intent is inferred by comparing observed trajectories with virtual route-following trajectories. This enables confirmation of true collision avoidance behaviour and extraction of the associated critical encounter scenarios. The proposed method is validated using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data from the high-traffic Øresund region, including the Helsingør-Helsingborg ferry corridor. Results on a labelled dataset show strong performance, achieving an F1-score of 0.8203 and 0.7443 in behaviour identification and encounter extraction, respectively. The findings demonstrate that the framework can robustly identify avoidance manoeuvres and capture critical encounters. Moreover, the proposed behaviour identification method is further applied in various navigational environments to verify its generalisation. The proposed critical encounter extraction framework provides empirically grounded insights into MASS development and testing, maritime situational awareness enhancement, and traffic management.

title: Examining impacts of tradable credit schemes on delivery services using an agent- and activity-based simulation framework
abstract: This paper presents a generalized Tradable Credit Scheme (TCS) framework for urban logistics. We rigorously compare an integrated market (MoLoCo), where urban mobility and last-mile delivery activities share a unified currency (Coins), against a sector-specific market (LoCo) with an independent emission cap for logistics. This study explores the regulatory effectiveness of these frameworks and evaluates the efficacy of adaptive operational strategies employed by a monopoly logistics provider. Using an agent- and activity-based simulation for Munich, Germany, we evaluate regulatory effectiveness and adaptive logistics strategies. Results indicate that MoLoCo framework benefits from a “Coupling Effect,” where the mode shift to low-emission travel modes stabilizes the Coin market prices, yet this triggers a “Green Logistics Paradox” by stimulating online shopping. Conversely, LoCo framework generates high Coin market prices that force decarbonization but risk a “Reverse Modal Shift,” driving cost-sensitive users back to physical stores and worsening congestion. Regarding logistics strategies, fleet electrification is cost-effective but fails to mitigate congestion. True spatial efficiency is achieved only through cargo bikes in the dense city center. We therefore propose a sequential TCS implementation roadmap: initiate sector-specific regulation to enforce technological adoption, then transition to an integrated market to maximize societal welfare.

title: Stochastic two-echelon vehicle routing with mobile satellites: Adaptive large neighborhood search with stochastic approximation scheduling
abstract: This paper studies the stochastic multi-commodity multi-depot two-echelon vehicle routing problem with mobile satellites (3M-2E-SVRP), where first-echelon vehicles serve as mobile transfer points for second-echelon deliveries under synchronization and time-window constraints. Travel and service times are modeled as independent truncated log-normal random variables in controlled stochastic benchmark instances. To solve the problem, we develop SAS-ALNS, an adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm that integrates deterministic approximation scheduling with stochastic approximation scheduling to evaluate feasibility, reliability, and expected failure costs during the search. Two stochastic planning perspectives are considered: a penalty-based model (PBM), which minimizes deterministic routing cost plus expected failed-delivery penalties, and a chance-constrained model (CCM), which imposes minimum customer-level on-time service probabilities under the modeled uncertainty. Computational experiments show that deterministic planning substantially underestimates late-arrival risk: under stochastic evaluation, deterministic solutions incur high expected failure costs and leave 27.1% of customers below a 95% success-probability threshold. PBM and CCM reduce expected failure costs by approximately 96% while achieving average customer success probabilities above 99%. SAS closely matches Monte Carlo simulation for both central and upper-tail arrival-time statistics while requiring substantially less evaluation time. Representative in-search comparisons with simulation-based candidate evaluation further show that SAS provides a favorable balance between solution quality, reliability stability, and computational effort. The results show that distribution-based stochastic schedule evaluation can be embedded efficiently into ALNS and improve the reliability of synchronized mobile-satellite routing decisions within the controlled benchmark and independence assumptions considered.

title: Multi-level optimization for the deployment of battery swapping in inland waterways
abstract: Containerized battery swapping offers a promising pathway to zero-emission inland waterway transport. However, its deployment requires coordinated decisions among actors with conflicting objectives. We introduce a multi-level optimization model with three actors: a policymaker who allocates subsidies to maximize adoption, an infrastructure developer who selects station locations to maximize profit, and fleet operators who minimize operating costs. We formulate this as a multi-level optimization problem, reduce it to a bilevel program via Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions, and solve it using an iterative bilevel decomposition and a problem-specific large neighborhood search. Experiments on the Dutch–Belgian inland waterway corridor show that a market equilibrium cannot exist without public intervention, the optimal subsidy mix depends on the available budget, and that within an intermediate price range the minimum budget for full adoption remains stable. Sensitivity analyses on costs, battery range, and network size are reported together with an alternative emissions-reduction objective.

title: Simulation-based Bayesian optimization for large-scale dynamic lane allocation
abstract: The current traffic research highly relies on Simulation-Based Optimization (SBO) to evaluate complex operational strategies. However, large-scale network problems often involve hundreds of control decisions that make the search space extremely high-dimensional and computationally prohibitive. This study develops an advanced Bayesian Optimization (BO) method for the large-scale SBO and applies it to solve the Dynamic Lane Allocation (DLA) problem, which grants ride-sharing vehicles conditional access to Dedicated Bus Lanes (DBLs) with allocation decisions varying across both location and time. As a result, the problem requires binary decisions across hundreds of space–time units, creating an extremely high-dimensional, combinatorial search space that existing optimization methods cannot handle efficiently. To address this challenge, we introduce a Grouped Automatic Relevance Determination (GARD) Hamming kernel that separates temporal and spatial relevance in the Gaussian Process (GP) surrogate, a dynamic group-aware dimension-reduction mechanism that identifies influential regions of the solution space, and a trust-region adaptation tailored to binary decisions to improve sampling efficiency. These components are combined with hybrid candidate generation and mixed batch sampling to enhance robustness under limited simulation budgets. The method is evaluated using a trip-based Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD) multimodal simulator on both a controlled virtual grid and the large-scale Barcelona network. Results show that the proposed BO approach consistently converges faster, achieves higher solution quality, and maintains feasibility under strict bus-service constraints compared with metaheuristic methods. The framework also demonstrates stable performance across varied OD patterns and scalability to real-world city networks.On the large-scale Barcelona network, the proposed method achieves, on average, a 14.2% lower final objective and 2.16 × faster convergence than Large Neighborhood Search (LNS), as well as a 1.1% lower final objective and 1.52 × faster convergence than Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS). These findings highlight the potential of the proposed method to support efficient decision-making in large-scale, binary, network-level traffic optimization.

title: Achieving net-zero emissions in logistics and operations: The net zero plus framework
abstract: Today, achieving net zero in logistics and operations is a top agenda for almost all organizations. In this context, there is no doubt that enabling technologies are critical for facilitating decarbonization (e.g., emissions reduction, offset, and removal). Moreover, fulfilling the net-zero goal naturally requires the participation of all stakeholders, within and beyond the traditional supply chains. This paper aims to critically examine the relevant studies on net-zero emissions in the operations and logistics literature, with the focal points on different major stakeholders (e.g., non-governmental organizations, governments, investors, service providers, supply chains, and consumers) as well as the role of enabling technologies. We also examine several real-world practices implemented by prominent firms (such as Apple, Amazon, and Nike). Based on the findings of literature review and observed practices, we establish a novel “Net Zero Plus” framework, where we highlight the underexplored potential of enabling technologies as a key “plus” to help achieve net-zero emissions. We further develop several propositions. Finally, we identify several research-practice gaps and then establish a real-practice driven future research agenda.

title: Equitable and visually attractive arc routing for residential waste collection with heterogeneous fleets
abstract: The residential waste collection problem (RWCP) is an arc routing problem in which multiple vehicles must service street segments while adhering to capacity and working-time constraints, with the possibility of multiple visits to landfills. In practice, route plans should be not only cost-efficient but also equitable across vehicles and visually attractive. This study addresses a multi-vehicle RWCP with heterogeneous fleets, where vehicles may differ in capacity and driver efficiency, and where route costs incorporate turn penalties. We formulate the problem as a mixed capacitated arc routing problem with intermediate facilities, in which service requirements are defined on both arcs (directed street segments) and edges (undirected street segments), and propose a hierarchical graph-partitioning-based matheuristic (H-GPM) to solve it. The proposed framework decomposes the problem into three stages: vehicle-level balanced clustering, trip-level capacitated clustering, and trip-level routing. At the vehicle level, it combines graph coarsening, Steiner tree-based route-cost estimation, initial solution construction, and local improvement to generate workload-balanced and spatially coherent task assignments. At the trip level, vehicle-specific subgraphs are partitioned into capacity-feasible trips, and routing decisions are determined by lexicographic MILP models that first minimize arc overlap and subsequently route cost. Computational experiments show that, compared with baseline methods for homogeneous fleets, H-GPM produces workload-balanced solutions while substantially improving visual attractiveness, particularly by reducing spatial overlap among vehicle routes. For heterogeneous fleets, H-GPM effectively accounts for turn penalties, vehicle capacities, driver efficiencies, and multi-trip operations, producing feasible and workload-balanced solutions. The evaluation of the embedded route-cost estimation procedure further supports the reliability of the proposed framework.

title: Constrained reinforcement learning for the dynamic inventory routing problem under stochastic supply and demand
abstract: Green hydrogen has multiple use cases and is produced from renewable energy, such as solar or wind energy. It can be stored in large quantities, decoupling renewable energy generation from its use, and is therefore considered essential for achieving a climate-neutral economy. The intermittency of renewable energy generation and the stochastic nature of demand are, however, challenging factors for the dynamic planning of hydrogen storage and transportation. This holds particularly in the early-adoption phase when hydrogen distribution occurs through vehicle-based networks. We therefore address the Dynamic Inventory Routing Problem (DIRP) under stochastic supply and demand with direct deliveries for the vehicle-based distribution of hydrogen. To solve this problem, we propose a Constrained Reinforcement Learning (CRL) framework that integrates constraints into the learning process and incorporates parameterized post-decision state value predictions. Additionally, we introduce Lookahead-based CRL (LCRL), which improves decision-making over a multi-period horizon to enhance short-term planning while maintaining the value predictions. Our computational experiments demonstrate the efficacy of CRL and LCRL across diverse instances. Our learning methods provide near-optimal solutions on small scale instances that are solved via value iteration. Furthermore, both methods outperform typical deep learning approaches such as Proximal Policy Optimization, as well as classical inventory heuristics, such as (s,S)-policy-based and Power-of-Two-based heuristics. Furthermore, LCRL achieves a 10% improvement over CRL on average, albeit with higher computational requirements. Analyses of optimal replenishment policies reveal that accounting for stochastic supply and demand influences these policies, showing the importance of our addition to the DIRP.

title: The latency location-or-routing problem
abstract: This paper introduces the latency location-or-routing problem (LLoRP); a variant of the location-or-routing problem (LoRP) and an extension of the latency location-routing problem. The LLoRP consists of selecting (opening) a set of depots to serve a set of customers, which can be visited as part of routes also to be decided. The maximum number of depots to open is assumed to be exogenous. For the customers lying within a certain coverage range from an open depot, direct service is an alternative. A set of capacitated homogeneous vehicles is available to be assigned to the selected depots as needed. The goal is to minimize the sum of the waiting times of the customers for being served (latency). Several customer-centric applications of the LLoRP are discussed. Three mixed-integer-linear-programming formulations are developed and two lower bounds on the optimal latency value are devised. A tradeoff between LLoRP and LoRP is considered within a bi-objective modeling framework that is tackled using the ε − constrained method. An outcome of this analysis are compact formulations for the standard LoRP. This type of model is in itself a novelty for that problem. Finally, extensive computational results are discussed to assess the relevance of the LLoRP and the efficacy of the models and bounds proposed. The results highlight multiple distinguishing features of the LLoRP while identifying the most promising optimization models to use. They also provide strong evidence for the relevance of looking into tradeoff solutions when a cost-oriented objective becomes of interest in addition to latency.

title: Securing the flow: Strategic storage and corridor design for maritime energy security under chokepoint disruptions
abstract: Maritime disruption planning requires joint decisions on strategic storage and transport capacity before corridor conditions are known. We develop a two-stage stochastic multi-commodity network-design model in which a national energy-security planner selects corridor commitments, port–commodity inventories, and optional storage expansion, then routes crude oil, LNG, LPG, and fertilizer through scenario-dependent flows. The formulation combines commodity admissibility, decision-dependent probabilities, corridor concentration limits, and mean–CVaR risk. It admits an exact MILP reformulation; a scenario-wise multi-cut Benders implementation serves as an independent verification tool. In the 729-scenario verification, the extensive form is faster than the Benders implementation. In a data-anchored, stylized India-inspired case study, stochastic modelling improves on the expected-value policy by about 1.35%, and decision-dependent probabilities are worth 0.67% at the analyst-set exposure scale. Commodity service is heterogeneous: crude and fertilizer remain fully served, while LNG and LPG reach worst positive-probability service of 34.6% and 33.3%, respectively. Under medium assumed capex, storage expansion adds 1,775 normalised capacity units at seven predefined port–commodity pairs and reduces active corridor commitments from 21 to 20. The calibrated binary Hormuz–Bab incidence probabilities factorise exactly. Across 168 primary fixed-marginal cells, dependence changes economic exposure without making the independence-optimised policy suboptimal; selected capacity and commitment-cost stresses change first-stage decisions, with maximum mechanism regret of 1.1673%.

title: Non-stop train systems to alleviate the accessibility and commercial speed trade-off: An analytical framework and optimal planning
abstract: Balancing accessibility and commercial speed is a fundamental challenge in passenger rail systems: more frequent stops improve first- and last-mile access but reduce commercial speed through stop-induced in-vehicle time losses. This study analyzes a non-stop modular train system with the potential to alleviate this structural trade-off. In this system, the main train body maintains cruising speed, while modular vehicles dynamically decouple and recouple at intermediate stations to enable passenger boarding and alighting. We develop an analytical framework to evaluate total passenger travel time, including access, waiting, and in-vehicle components, under both conventional and non-stop operations, and apply it to the KTX Gyeongbu Line, a major high-speed rail corridor in Korea. Under the same average station spacing and fleet size, non-stop operations reduce waiting time by 38 % and in-vehicle travel time by 36 %, lowering total passenger travel time from 2.66 to 2.07 h, a 22 % reduction, by eliminating intermediate dwell time and repeated acceleration and braking of the main train body. Extending the analysis to optimal planning, we determine the station spacing and fleet size that minimize total daily cost, defined as the sum of passenger time, operating, and infrastructure costs, for both conventional and non-stop cases. Under peak-demand constraints, the optimized non-stop system achieves a 43 % smaller optimal station spacing and a 22 % lower total daily cost than the optimized conventional system. The results indicate that even optimized conventional designs remain constrained by the inherent accessibility–speed trade-off, whereas optimized non-stop operations can improve both spatio-temporal accessibility and commercial speed.

title: Bus lane design problem with Steiner tree constraints to account for road congestion
abstract: This paper addresses the design of a bus lane network that connects key bus stops (or bus interchanges) while minimizing overall traffic impact. We seek a Steiner tree configuration of bus lanes that maximizes benefits for transit passengers (minimizing total passenger-hours) while simultaneously minimizing the adverse impact on private vehicles (minimizing additional vehicle-hours). This problem is formulated as a bi-level program that incorporates a user equilibrium (UE) condition for private vehicles as a constraint. To navigate the vast solution space efficiently, we introduce an innovative sensitivity analysis method based on bush-based UE assignment. This method is embedded within a link-swapping Tabu search heuristic, enabling the proposed optimization framework to scale to large, realistic urban networks. Numerical experiments conducted on the 215-node Gifu City network demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of our approach.

title: An energy-efficient coordinated procurement, production, and batch delivery scheduling system for sustainable operations with Net-Zero emissions
abstract: Over the last decade, rising energy prices, global warming, the harmful effects of energy use, and carbon emissions have highlighted the importance of energy and carbon efficiency. In response to local energy regulations and carbon-sensitive markets, manufacturers and logistics organizations are actively seeking effective methods to improve energy and carbon efficiency. This research enhances supply chain planning and scheduling by combining procurement, production, and delivery decisions to support sustainable operations through simultaneously optimizing costs, energy consumption, and carbon emissions. An E nergy- E fficient C oordinated P roduction- D istribution S ystem ( EE-CPDS ) is designed, accounting for a flexible job-shop scheduling environment with inter-machine transport times and sequence-dependent setup times to reflect real production configurations. To address the computational challenge, we propose a novel multi-objective adaptive search memetic algorithm (MOASMA) that outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of solution quality, i.e., generating global solutions closer to true Pareto front with average hypervolume (HV) value of 0.7131 and Inverted Generational Distance Plus (IGD + ) value of 0.0249 across nine test instances, which is further endorsed by nonparametric statistical analysis. Among the instances solved by all competing algorithms, MOASMA provides better solutions for 77% of them. The correctness and effectiveness of the developed algorithm are verified by comparing the results with an exact solver (Gurobi), which is effective for small and medium-sized instances, while MOASMA proves efficient for larger-scale problems. The proposed system and algorithm will assist enterprises in solving practical-sized instances while rationalizing coordinated procurement, production, and distribution decisions that support sustainable operations and drive progress toward net-zero emissions.

title: Optimizing freight rail electrification: A framework for charge station selection and battery charge/swap scheduling
abstract: Battery-electric freight trains are promising for decarbonization by providing zero-emission transportation alternatives. Successful adoption of battery-electric freight trains depends on an efficient electrification strategy, involving infrastructure setup and charging scheduling. The study presents a comprehensive model for the optimal design of charging infrastructure and charge scheduling for trains. To provide greater recharging flexibility, we allow a battery to be either charged or swapped at a deployed station, and each train can carry multiple batteries. This problem is formulated as a mixed-integer linear programming model with a Rectangle Piecewise Linear Approximation (PLA) technique. To obtain strategic and tactical solutions, we develop two algorithms to solve the optimization problem: (1) a Fix Algorithm (FA), and (2) Benders Decomposition (BD) algorithm with extra feasibility cuts to speed up the procedure. In computational experiments, we use the original model with the PLA technique, and the two proposed algorithms. Statistical analysis verifies the modified BD algorithm with extra feasibility cuts performs best with respect to the objective function value in larger instances, closely followed by FA, and the PLA technique provides the least optimal solutions. Specifically, compared with the standard BD, the modified BD can reduce the objective function value by 11.73%, 30.92% and 51.58% on large, extra large and high-frequency instances, respectively. Sensitivity analysis is implemented to investigate the impact of delay penalty weight, charge rate, demand pattern and battery inventory. Finally, a case study is conducted to demonstrate the application of the proposed framework in a representative freight rail planning setting.

title: IoT-enabled packaging recycling adoption in circular packaging 4.0 supply chains under policy mechanisms
abstract: Achieving a circular economy (CE) is a critical societal challenge as packaging waste surges while recycling rates remain low. Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, such as RFID tracking and smart sorting, offer tools to improve recycling efficiency. The manufacturer can choose between the traditional packaging recycling (TPR) and IoT-enabled packaging recycling (IPR) modes, which differ in cost structure, operational efficiency, and environmental impact. Government subsidies for Packaging 4.0 further influence recycling adoption decisions. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of the IPR mode and subsidy impacts, yielding three key findings. First, while the IPR mode generally increases the recycling rate, it may unexpectedly lead to higher landfill volumes under certain conditions, highlighting unintended environmental consequences of technological adoption. Second, incorporating government subsidies into the decision framework demonstrates that uniform subsidies fail to account for industry cost differences, whereas targeted subsidies lead to more efficient resource allocation and enhanced social welfare. Finally, a case illustration of Australia’s B2C packaging industry explores how the interaction of IoT adoption and environmental subsidies optimizes the IPR mode. The findings provide actionable insights for policymakers and industry leaders to design adaptive policies that balance financial and environmental goals.

title: Resilience assessment for China’s crude oil shipping network considering maritime chokepoint disruptions
abstract: Maritime chokepoints face increasing external disruptions from geopolitical conflicts, climate change, and sea accidents, which impose significant risks on global shipping networks and economic prosperity. This study proposes an optimization-based analytical framework to examine the dynamic behavior of network resilience across both disruption and recovery phases. Distinguished from traditional studies that rely on centrality-based indexes to determine critical nodes, the proposed framework identifies worst-case scenario by evaluating specific node failure sequences that induces the maximum resilience performance drop. A dual-optimization framework is then developed to determine the optimal recovery sequence. This framework maximizes the marginal improvement in system performance while explicitly accounting for the node-level recovery priorities. The proposed framework is empirically applied to China’s crude oil shipping network, constructed using voyage records derived from AIS that relevant to crude oil tankers serving China’s import trade. The analysis identifies a non-linear relationship between resilience loss during the recovery stage and the level of alternative capacity of disrupted maritime chokepoints. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that when critical chokepoints are disrupted, re-routing is not necessarily preferable to targeted recovery efforts. Based on these insights, this study provides a strategic decision-support tool for shipping companies to optimize routing designs and it offers a framework for national governments to safeguard energy security by identifying which chokepoints require prioritized diplomatic cooperation and infrastructure investments.

title: Incentive-based strategies for road–waterway city logistics: A single-leader multi-follower game-theoretic framework
abstract: Urban freight transportation contributes substantially to congestion, pollution, and operational inefficiencies, particularly in dense urban areas where delivery activities remain strongly dependent on road transport. To address these impacts, policymakers are increasingly exploring incentive-based mechanisms that promote modal shifts toward alternative freight services within multimodal city logistics systems, while this study focuses specifically on the shift from road delivery to inland waterway transport. The effectiveness of such policies critically depends on the strategic interactions among multiple stakeholders. We therefore propose a single-leader multi-follower game-theoretic framework involving a transportation authority, logistics service providers (LSPs), and end customers. The transportation authority acts as the leader and designs the waterway subsidy policy to promote road-to-waterway modal shift under fiscal constraints. The LSPs act as followers and maximize their own profits by determining service prices and road–waterway delivery allocations. Customer demand is modeled endogenously through a discrete choice model, and the joint response of the LSPs is characterized by a generalized Nash equilibrium. Finally, three implementation strategies for deploying road-to-waterway modal-shift policies are examined and compared in a case study of Amsterdam, providing insights into their relative efficiency and practical implications.

title: Synchronizing airport check-in and security services through urban air mobility: A preference analysis of air passengers’ choices under time uncertainty
abstract: This paper investigates the propensity of air passengers to use Urban Air Mobility (UAM) airport shuttle services that integrate synchronized baggage check-in and security screening traditionally performed at airports. A stated choice experiment was designed, allowing people to choose between conventional airport access modes and UAM shuttle services under varying travel conditions. To account for travel time uncertainty associated with ground access to UAM vertiports, a random parameter hybrid logit model incorporating cumulative prospect theory was estimated. The results indicate that employed individuals and frequent air travelers are more likely to be the early adopters of synchronized passenger services. Passengers traveling with companions, carrying multiple pieces of baggage, or undertaking long-distance trips, also show a stronger preference for UAM airport shuttles. In particular, streamlining baggage check-in and security screening, together with future ride incentives, significantly increase the probability of using UAM airport shuttles. These findings provide valuable insights for operators and policymakers seeking to design passenger-centered UAM airport shuttle services and enhance integration with existing air transport systems.

title: Corporate social responsibility incentives in supply chains under pricing authority: The role of reverse factoring
abstract: Reverse factoring is a buyer-led supply chain finance mechanism that can alleviate the financial constraints faced by small and medium-sized suppliers and improve their capacity to invest in corporate social responsibility (CSR). However, improved access to financing does not necessarily translate into CSR investment, because the supplier’s incentive also depends on the allocation of wholesale-pricing authority and its ability to retain the returns generated by CSR. We develop an analytical model of a two-tier supply chain under demand uncertainty that integrates reverse factoring, endogenous wholesale pricing, order quantity, and supplier CSR effort. We compare two pricing structures: supplier-led pricing, in which the supplier determines the wholesale price and CSR effort, and retailer-led pricing, in which the retailer sets the wholesale price before the supplier chooses CSR effort. The results show that reverse factoring reduces financing-inclusive production and CSR costs, thereby improving the financial feasibility of CSR investment. Nevertheless, positive CSR effort depends on threshold conditions involving CSR effectiveness, CSR cost, production cost, and supplier margin. Supplier-led pricing generally supports CSR investment over a wider parameter region and induces higher CSR effort because the supplier can retain a larger share of the demand-enhancing value CSR generates. Under retailer-led pricing, wholesale-price compression may offset the financing benefit and reduce or eliminate the supplier’s incentive to invest. These findings demonstrate that the sustainability impact of reverse factoring depends on its interaction with pricing authority and surplus allocation. Managers should therefore coordinate financing arrangements with wholesale-pricing policies that preserve sufficient supplier incentives while maintaining overall supply chain performance.

title: Optimization approaches for a fair multi-source capacitated facility location problem
abstract: We incorporate a fairness measure, known as the conditional β -mean in location theory, into the Multi-Source Capacitated Facility Location Problem (MSCFLP). The conditional β -mean measures the average distance traveled by the (100 · β )% of demand units that face the longest travel distances to a facility. Minimizing the conditional β -mean results in a less conservative and more flexible approach than a standard maximum distance minimization. We term the resulting problem the Fair MSCFLP, and we develop five mathematical formulations to model it: two bilevel models, one bilinear model, and two Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulations. We also devise two matheuristics: a Variable MILP Neighborhood Descent ( VMND ) algorithm, and a ternary search-based approach ( Ternary ). Extensive computational experiments conducted on benchmark data sets for the MSCFLP, consisting of up to 1000 facilities and 1000 customers, show that an off-the-shelf solver can solve, in reasonable computing times, only small instances. Both matheuristics found the optimal solution to each small instance within a few seconds. The experimental analysis indicates that no matheuristic outperforms the other across all instances: depending on the size, one matheuristic generally outperforms the other when run with a time limit. Ternary usually outperforms VMND solving instances that comprise up to 500 facilities and 500 customers, whereas VMND produces solutions of considerably better quality on larger instances.

title: Topology-aware preconditioning for UAV logistics infrastructure and distributed swarm scheduling
abstract: Abstract In large-scale UAV logistics systems, distributed scheduling has emerged as a key approach to overcoming the scalability limitations of centralized architectures. However, existing studies primarily focus on improving optimization algorithms, while largely overlooking the fundamental constraints imposed by the underlying communication topology. In real urban environments, heterogeneous spatial distributions often lead to poorly connected networks, which in turn become a critical bottleneck limiting distributed coordination efficiency.This paper investigates how communication topology shapes distributed scheduling performance from the perspective of coupling transportation infrastructure and information interaction. Building upon algebraic graph theory and distributed optimization, we establish a quantitative relationship between network connectivity and the convergence rate of cooperative errors, and show that, under construction cost constraints, system performance is subject to an inherent structural upper bound. To address this limitation, we propose a topology optimization method that enhances connectivity under realistic spatial constraints, and further develop a topology-aware distributed scheduling framework that enables joint design of infrastructure and coordination mechanisms.Experiments based on real-world logistics networks demonstrate that modest topology enhancements can accelerate system convergence and reduce scheduling delays under high-load conditions. Ablation studies further confirm that network connectivity plays a key role in determining overall system performance.Overall, this work reveals the mechanism linking transportation infrastructure topology to distributed coordination efficiency, and provides a principled approach to upgrading infrastructure from passive physical assets to active computational topology resources, offering theoretical support for the integration of computing and networking in future intelligent transportation systems.

title: A deep reinforcement learning-based algorithm for regional drone routing problem with nonlinear fuel consumption
abstract: With the boom of e-commerce and increasing policy support, regional logistics serving medium- and short-distance transportation have grown rapidly. Large fuel-powered drones are increasingly adopted in this field due to their flexibility and efficiency, yet their deployment has raised concerns regarding pollutant emissions and environmental sustainability. To balance logistics efficiency with environmental responsibility, this paper proposes a regional drone routing problem using large fuel-powered drones, accounting for nonlinear fuel consumption and multiple pollutant emissions. The problem is formulated as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming model to minimize the total cost, including fuel consumption cost, pollutant emission cost, and operational cost. To accurately estimate fuel consumption, a nonlinear fuel consumption function is formulated by comprehensively considering variable payload, fluctuating fuel load, empty weight, the entire flight process, and wind. A deep reinforcement learning-based algorithm, namely a double-deep Q-network with attention mechanism based large neighborhood search algorithm, is designed to solve the model. The effectiveness of the algorithm and the nonlinear fuel consumption function is validated by comparative experiments on simulated instances, and then the impacts of refueling availability and wind conditions on the total cost are further investigated. Furthermore, based on a real-world case, this paper shows that drones can reduce the total cost, while sensitivity analyses evaluate the impact of key factors on environmental and economic performance. The results indicate that the proposed model and algorithm can effectively enhance operational efficiency and environmental performance.

title: Optimal menu pricing strategies for on-demand service platforms
abstract: On-demand service platforms such as Uber, DoorDash, and Lyft are increasingly adopting menu-based pricing strategies that combine a pay-per-use option with a premium membership plan. Memberships provide discounted transaction fees and enhanced service quality in exchange for an upfront fee, yet it remains unclear when these strategies are viable and how membership and per-transaction fees should be optimally set. This study develops a profit-maximization model that determines optimal membership fees and per-transaction charges while accounting for customer heterogeneity in service valuation and usage frequency. Users self-select between membership and pay-per-use under fixed discount and quality parameters. The analysis reveals that discount rates and service quality affect market structure in fundamentally different ways. For discounts, we identify a critical threshold: below it, platforms charge higher per-transaction fees than membership fees, resulting in only two customer segments (premium users and non-users) with transaction-based revenues; beyond it, platforms can effectively implement menu pricing with three segments (premium, regular, and non-users) and membership-driven revenues. For quality, the relationship is non-monotonic: moderate quality levels maximize both premium user adoption and platform profitability, while higher quality investments incur provision costs that erode margins and shift market structure toward regular-user dominance. These findings define a narrow viability zone where menu pricing can function effectively. An extension that jointly optimizes pricing and service design reveals that unconstrained platforms abandon menu pricing in favor of quality-based differentiation with per-transaction fees, confirming that menu pricing is a second-best strategy whose value arises precisely when discount and quality levels are externally constrained. The study provides a structured framework for evaluating menu pricing strategies and actionable guidance for platform managers.
